DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
This action is in response to the papers filed June 29, 2021.  Currently, claims 21-29 are pending.
Priority
This application is a CON of 15/517,215 filed 09/18/2017, now PAT 11072828 which is a 371 of PCT/US2015/054194 and claims priority to provisional application 62/060,503 filed October 6, 2014.
Drawings
The drawings are acceptable.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 21-29 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
35 U.S.C. § 101 requires that to be patent-eligible, an invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception. M.P.E.P. § 2106. Regarding judicial exceptions, “[p]henomena of nature, though just discovered, mental processes, and abstract intellectual concepts are not patentable, as they are the basic tools of scientific and technological work.” Gottschalk v. Benson, 409 U.S. 63, 67 (1972); see also M.P.E.P. § 2106, part II.
Based upon consideration of the claims as a whole, as well as consideration of elements/steps recited in addition to the judicial exception, the present claims fail to meet the elements required for patent eligibility.
Step 1
The claimed invention is directed to a process.
Question 2A
The claims are taken to be directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature and a natural phenomenon.
Claim 1 is directed to “a method for treating PTSD in a subject comprising administering a PTSD treatment to a subject predicted to have PTSD” where predicting PTSD by measuring DNA methylation at a CpG located in 3’ UTR of SKA2, identifying the genotype at SNP rs7208505 and predicting PTSD using a linear model.
Claim 1 is directed to a process that involves the judicial exceptions of an abstract idea (i.e. using a linear model and predicting PTSD) and a law of nature/natural phenomenon (i.e., the natural correlation between DNA methylation and the genotype at SNP rs7208505 and risk of PTSD).
Here, Claim 1 requires performing the step of “measuring the DNA methylation level at a CpG in the 3’ UTR of SKA2 and identifying the genotype at SNP rs7208505 as using a linear model to predict PTSD.    The specification teaches that data was downloaded (see page 31, line 5).  Using a linear model to determine PTSD is an abstract idea. This judicial exception is of the type identified by the Courts as an abstract idea akin to the following cases: “the collection, analysis, and display of available information in a particular field” (.Electric Power Group (Fed. Cir. 2016)); “the broad concept of monitoring audit log data” (FairWarning IP LLC (Fed Cir 2016)); Improvement to computer-related technology (e.g., computer functionality) (Enfish LLC (Fed. Cir. 2016)); “specific improvements in computer technology which go beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activities” (BASCOM (Fed. Cir. 2016)); “the incorporation of claimed rules that 'improved [the] existing technological process' by allowing the automation of further tasks. (McRO Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2016)) and “classifying and storing digital images in an organized manner”
As summarized in FairWarning, the courts have explained that the realm of abstract ideas includes collecting information, including when limited to particular content. (.Electric Power (Fed. Cir. 2016) (collecting cases listed above)). The courts have also treated analyzing information by steps people go through in their minds, or by mathematical algorithms, without more, as essentially mental processes within the abstract-idea category. And the courts have found that merely presenting the results of abstract processes of collecting and analyzing information, without more (such as identifying a particular tool for presentation), is abstract as an ancillary part of such collection and analysis. Id. Here, the claims are directed to a combination of these abstract-idea categories. Specifically, the claims here are directed to the collection of methylation and genotype data, and the mathematical analysis of that data, without significantly more.
The claims also involve the judicial exception of a law of nature/natural phenomenon.  The claims are based on the correlation between DNA methylation at a CpG site in the 3’UTR of SKA2 and the genotype at SNP rs7208505 and risk of PTSD.  The claims require predicting PTSD using a linear model.  As in Prometheus, the relation itself is a natural phenomenon that exists apart from any human action.
Question 2A Prong II
The exception is not integrated into a practical application of the exception.  The claims do not recite any additional elements that integrate the exception into a practical application of the exception.  While the claim recites obtaining a sample and genotyping, this is not an integration of the exception into a practical application.  Instead, these elements are data gathering required to perform the method.
With respect to the limitation of “administering a PTSD treatment to a subject predicted to have PTSD” this is a mere statement of “apply it”.  MPEP 2106.04(d)(2)(a) provides treatments must be “particular” such that they do not encompass all applications of the judicial exception.  This administration step of “administering a PTSD treatment” is not particular and is instead merely instructions to “apply” the exception in a generic way.  Thus, the administration step does not integrate the predicting step into a practical application.
Thus, the claim is “directed to” the exception.
Question 2B
The second step of Alice involves determining whether the remaining elements, either in isolation or combination with the other non patent ineligible elements, are sufficient to “’transform the nature of the claim’ into a patent eligible application” Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355 (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1297).
The claims are not sufficiently defined to provide a method which is significantly more from a statement of a natural principle for at least these reasons:
The claims do not include applying the judicial exception, or by use of, a particular machine.  The claims do not tie the steps to a “particular machine and therefore do not meet the machine or transformation test on these grounds.  The use of machines generally does not impose a meaningful limit on claim scope.
The claims are not considered to recite any additional steps or elements that amount to significantly more than route in and conventional activity and the steps/elements in the claims do not add something “significantly more” so as to render the claim patent eligible.
The claims broadly recite steps for measuring the DNA methylation level at a CpG located at position 57187729 of chromosome 17 and the genotype at SNP rs7208505 are not considered to add something significantly more to the judicial exceptions because the step is recited at a high level of generality.  Methods of obtaining a nucleic acid sample and determining the presence of methylation level sand polymorphisms in the sample were well-known routine and conventional at the time the invention was made.  The claims also do not add a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field.
Perlegen teaches analysis of the ss24087298 mutation (namely the rs7208505 mutation).  Perlegen teaches identifying the G/A mutation at rs7208505.  The A allele is the major allele found in 56-78% of the population (see the three populations analyzed).  Perlegen also provides the genotypes for each of the individuals.  For the individuals with the A/A genotype, no methylation would be present as the nucleotide cannot be methylated.
Mehta teaches investigating DNA methylation profiles of the transcripts differentially regulated in either the PTSD case groups versus controls using the Illumina 450K Human Methylation array.  The instant specification teaches that the CpG at 57187729 of chromosome 17 is located on the Illumina 450K Bead Chip.  Mehta teaches that the CpG at 57187729 of chromosome 17 is not differentially methylated (see Supplemental Table 1).  Thus, methylation level of the CpG in the PTSD cases, where the sex and age of the patients was known, and the controls were determined even though they were found to be unmethylated.  Since Mehta did not identify any methylation, the genotype at the SNP rs7208505 was inherently the wild-type T which is not methylated.   Mehta teaches trauma questionnaires were used to measure stress/anxieties including sexual, physical and emotional abuse, and emotional and physical neglect (page 8306).
The step of obtaining a nucleic acid sample and analyzing the nucleic acids in the sample to determining the methylation level and genotype are data gathering steps necessary to use the judicial exceptions.  It merely tells the users of the method to determine the methylation level and genotype of a sample without further specification as to how the sample should be analyzed.   The claim does not recite a new, innovative method for such determination.  The predicting step is also a data manipulation method.  As such, the steps constitute insignificant, pre-solution activity.  The steps merely instruct the practitioner to use any well-known, conventional technique with generic reagents to detect the methylation level and polymorphism.
With regard to the element of a linear model that utilizes the DNA methylation level, genotype, age and sex, this element is generically recited and is insufficient.  It does not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s).  As the courts have explained, the use of generic computer elements like a microprocessor or user interface do not alone transform an otherwise abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter. See DDR Holdings (Fed. Cir. 2014).
Further, the Alice Corp decision informs in regards to method claims: Use of an unspecified, generic computer does not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention. Thus, the claim does not amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself’. (Federal Register Vol. 79, No. 241, 74628 Tuesday, December 16, 2014).  Here, the claim is not specific to a computer but relies upon a generic linear model.  The instant claims recite only generic linear models in conventional use.  It may be impractical and tedious to analyze bioinformatics data without an electronic computer, but it is not impossible.
Further the courts have found that:
“Though that analysis can be difficult, it is facilitated somewhat if, as here, the only physical step involves merely gathering data for the algorithm. As stated in In re Christensen, 478 F.2d 1392. 1394. 178 USPO 35. 37-38 1CCPA 1973): “Given that the method of solving a mathematical equation may not be the subject of patent protection, it follows that the addition of the old and necessary antecedent steps of establishing values for the variables in the equation cannot convert the unpatentable method to patentable subject matter.” Accord; In re Chatfield, (CCPA 1976). The reason for this was explained in In re Sarkar. “No mathematical equation can be used, as a practical matter, without establishing and substituting values for the variables expressed therein. Substitution of values dictated by the formula has thus been viewed as a form of mathematical step. If the steps of gathering and substituting values were alone sufficient, every mathematical equation, formula, or algorithm having any practical use would be per se subject to patenting as a process under § 101. Consideration of whether the substitution of specific values is enough to convert the disembodied ideas present in the formula into an embodiment of those ideas, or into an application of the formula, is foreclosed by the current state of the law”, (as cited in In re Grams, 888 F.2d 835 (CAFC 1989 at 840).
The claims further suffer from not applying the abstract idea in a meaningful way. These claims are considered mathematical relationships/formulas that are not applied in a specific way so as to render the claims practically applied, (see Benson or Parker v. Flook). The claims manipulate data using well-known, conventional techniques without adding a patent eligible application. Further action must be taken upon the results of the generic “analysis” or “linear model”.
In summation, the limitations of the claims, individually, and in ordered combination as a whole, do not rise to the level of significantly more than the judicial exception(s) identified above, and the claims are not patent eligible subject matter.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112-Scope of Enablement
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
Claims 21-29 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), first paragraph, because the specification, while being enabling for a method of measuring DNA methylation levels, detecting a genotype at SNP rs7208505, does not reasonably provide enablement for methods of predicting a subject has PTSD using a linear model that incorporates the measured DNA methylation level and genotype to predict PTSD in the subject.   The specification does not enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to use the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.
Factors to be considered in determining whether a disclosure meets the enablement requirement of 35 USC 112, first paragraph, have been described by the court in In re Wands, 8 USPQ2d 1400 (CA FC 1988).  Wands states at page 1404,
“Factors to be considered in determining whether a disclosure would require undue experimentation have been summarized by the board in Ex parte Forman. They include (1) the quantity of experimentation necessary, (2) the amount of direction or guidance presented, (3) the presence or absence of working examples, (4) the nature of the invention, (5) the state of the prior art, (6) the relative skill of those in the art, (7) the predictability or unpredictability of the art, and (8) the breadth of the claims.”
The nature of the invention and breadth of claims
Claims 21-29 are drawn to methods of predicting a subject has PTSD using a linear model that incorporates the measured DNA methylation level and genotype to predict PTSD in the subject.
The invention is in a class of invention which the CAFC has characterized as “the unpredictable arts such as chemistry and biology.”  Mycogen Plant Sci., Inc. v. Monsanto Co., 243 F.3d 1316, 1330 (Fed. Cir. 2001).
The unpredictability of the art and the state of the prior art
The art teaches analysis of methylation and genotypes in SAK2.  Perlegen teaches analysis of the ss24087298 mutation (namely the rs7208505 mutation).  Perlegen teaches identifying the G/A mutation at rs7208505.  The A allele is the major allele found in 56-78% of the population (see the three populations analyzed).  Perlegen also provides the genotypes for each of the individuals.  For the individuals with the A/A genotype, no methylation would be present as the nucleotide cannot be methylated.
Mehta teaches investigating DNA methylation profiles of the transcripts differentially regulated in either the PTSD case groups versus controls using the Illumina 450K Human Methylation array.  The instant specification teaches that the CpG at 57187729 of chromosome 17 is located on the Illumina 450K Bead Chip.  Mehta teaches that the CpG at 57187729 of chromosome 17 is not differentially methylated (see Supplemental Table 1).  Thus, methylation level of the CpG in the PTSD cases, where the sex and age of the patients was known, and the controls were determined even though they were found to be unmethylated.  Since Mehta did not identify any methylation, the genotype at the SNP rs7208505 was inherently the wild-type T which is not methylated.   Mehta teaches trauma questionnaires were used to measure stress/anxieties including sexual, physical and emotional abuse, and emotional and physical neglect (page 8306).
Guidance in the Specification.
The specification provides no evidence that the broad scope of the claims would enable the skilled artisan to practice the claimed invention as broadly as claimed.
The specification teaches methylation variation at rs7208505 represents the first genetic and epigenetic biomarker capable of predicting PTSD in a prospective manner with over 75% accuracy from blood (Page 29, lines 30-35).  The rs7208505 SNP and the cg13989295 are located at the same position in the genome such that the T/C variation is also measured for methylation of the variant C.
The specification analyzes and applies a suicide prediction model to PTSD.  The ability of the suicide prediction model to identify PTSD cases from the GTP cohort varied.  One model provided an AUC of 0.55 and p=0.24.  Another provided a significant value (see page 38).  Further an interactive model had a p-value of 0.066 (page 44).  Even more, no significant interactions were observed with the model with CTQ (see page 45).  Each model yielded different results and different significance.
Table 6 illustrates numerous CpG sites in the SKA2 region and their association with PTSD.  It is clear that only three of the 18 sites tested had a significant p-value association with methylation and PTSD.  Thus, it is unpredictable which DNA methylation levels in the 3’ UTR region of SKA2 may be used in the linear model to predict PTSD without further unpredictable and undue experimentation.
The guidance provided by the specification amounts to an invitation for the skilled artisan to try and follow the disclosed instructions to make and use the claimed invention.
Quantity of Experimentation
The quantity of experimentation in this area is extremely large since there is significant number of parameters which would have to be studied to enable the skilled artisan to predict PTSD in a subject using a linear model that incorporates any CpG dinucleotide methylation level from the 3’ UTR of SKA2 and genotype of rs7208505.  The evidence in the specification provides that only three of 18 studied CpG sites provide any significant association with PTSD.  The skilled artisan would be required to perform significant additional experimentation to determine which, if any CpG sites, aside from cg13989295 at the same position as rs7208505, would allow prediction of PTSD.
Further the specification does not provide a clear discussion of the linear model that would allow PTSD to be predicted.  The specification discusses numerous linear models, some that work and some that do not work to predict PTSD.  It is unpredictable what elements are required to be present to allow prediction of PTSD using DNA methylation and genotype analysis of rs7208505.
This would require significant inventive effort, with each of the many intervening steps, upon effective reduction to practice, not providing any guarantee of success in the succeeding steps.
Level of Skill in the Art
The level of skill in the art is deemed to be high.
Conclusion
Thus given the broad claims in an art whose nature is identified as unpredictable, the unpredictability of that art, the large quantity  of research required to define these unpredictable variables, the lack of guidance provided in the specification, the absence of a working example and the negative teachings in the prior art balanced only against the high skill level in the art, it is the position of the examiner that it would require undue experimentation for one of skill in the art to perform the method of the claim as broadly written.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
Claims 21-29 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claim 21 requires administering a PTSD treatment to a subjected predicted to have PTSED and diagnosed as such.  It is unclear what diagnosed as such means and requires.  The claim sets forth a using a linear model to predict PTSD in a subject but provides no guidance or antecedent basis for diagnosis of PTSD.  It is unclear what more is required for diagnosis that is not required for predicted to have PTSD.  Thus, “diagnosed as such” lacks proper antecedent basis.  Claims 22-29 are similarly indefinite as they depend on Claim 21.
Claim 28 is indefinite over “the difference in DNA methylation” because “the difference” lacks proper antecedent basis.  Claim 21 does not provide any difference, comparison or relationship.  Thus, it is unclear what difference in DNA methylation at SKA2 is referred to.  Clarification is required.
Double Patenting
The nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy (a policy reflected in the statute) so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees.  See In re Goodman, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); In re Longi, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985); In re Van Ornum, 686 F.2d 937, 214 USPQ 761 (CCPA 1982); In re Vogel, 422 F.2d 438, 164 USPQ 619 (CCPA 1970);and, In re Thorington, 418 F.2d 528, 163 USPQ 644 (CCPA 1969).
A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the conflicting application or patent is shown to be commonly owned with this application.  See 37 CFR 1.130(b).
Effective January 1, 1994, a registered attorney or agent of record may sign a terminal disclaimer.  A terminal disclaimer signed by the assignee must fully comply with 37 CFR 3.73(b).
An obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but an examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined claim is either anticipated by or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).  See e.g., In re Berg, 140 F.3d 1428, 46 USPQ2d 1226 (fed. Cir. 1998); In re Goodman, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); In re Longi, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985).
Claims 21-29 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-5, 7-13 of Patent 10,280,464 (reference application) in view of Khan, Arifulla (WO 2011/11927, September 29, 2011).
Although the conflicting claims are not identical, they are not patentable distinct from each other because Claims 21-29 of the instant application is generic to all that is recited in claims 1-5, 7-13 of Patent 10,280,464 (reference application).	The instant claims are generic to the three active method steps as required by claims in ‘464.  While the intended use of ‘464 is for suicide attempts and the instant claims are directed to PTSD, these two phenotypes are overlapping in scope.  Further, the active method steps do not require anything different.   The instant specification, repeatedly provides that a previously published SKA2 suicide prediction rule for PTSD resulted in a significant prediction of PTSD (see pages 43, page 59, lines 15-20, for example).
‘464 does not teach treating the patients predicted to have suicide.
However, Khan teaches suicide may be treated using antidepressants.
Therefore, it would have been prima facie obvious at the time the invention was made to have treated patients predicted to have PTSD or suicidal thoughts with well known treatments, as taught by Khan.  Therefore, the instant claims are obvious in view of the allowed claims in ‘464.
Claims 21-29 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-14 of Patent 11,072,828 (reference application) in view of Helton et al. (WO 2009/062134, May 14, 2009).
Although the conflicting claims are not identical, they are not patentable distinct from each other because Claims 21-29 of the instant application is generic to all that is recited in claims 1-14 of Patent 11,072,828 (reference application).	The instant claims are generic to the three active method steps as required by claims in ‘828.
‘828 does not teach treating the patients predicted to have PTSD.
However, Helton teaches patients predicted to have PTSD or diagnosed with PTSD may be treated.  Helton teaches current treatment options for PTSD include patient education, social support, and anxiety management through psychotherapy and psychopharmacologic intervention. Helton also teaches medications for treating PTSD include antidepressants and antipsychotic drugs. Paroxetine (Paxil) and sertraline (Zoloft) are currently the only medications that have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of PTSD.
Therefore, it would have been prima facie obvious at the time the invention was made to have treated patients predicted to have PTSD with well known PTSD treatments, as taught by Helton.  Therefore, the instant claims are obvious in view of the allowed claims in ‘828.
Conclusion
No claims allowable.
